pharm: Peptidomimetic inhibitor of HIV-1 protease that binds the protease active site, preventing cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors into functional proteins, so that immature, non-infectious viral particles are produced. Metabolized chiefly by CYP3A4 and is itself a CYP3A4 inhibitor, giving extensive drug interactions; renal excretion of poorly soluble drug predisposes to crystalluria and stones.
quick: 800 mg (usually two 400 mg capsules) orally every 8 hours
Empty stomach with water 1 h before or 2 h after a meal, OR with a light/low-fat meal
No adequate studies; use only if benefit justifies fetal risk - watch neonatal bilirubin
Do not breastfeed - HIV transmission risk; presence in human milk unknown
Not studied in renal impairment; ensure hydration to prevent stones/renal injury
Reduce to 600 mg every 8 h in mild-moderate cirrhosis; not studied in severe
No specific interaction described; counsel general adherence and hydration
Hydration/urinalysis for stones, bilirubin, LFTs, glucose/lipids, CBC for hemolysis
summary: Indinavir (Crixivan) is an HIV-1 protease inhibitor used in combination with other antiretroviral agents to treat HIV infection. The standard adult dose is 800 mg every 8 hours, taken on an empty stomach with water (1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal) or with a light low-fat meal, because a high-fat meal markedly reduces absorption. Its hallmark toxicity is nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis from poorly soluble drug crystallizing in the urinary tract, so patients must maintain ADEQUATE HYDRATION - at least 1.5 liters (about 48 ounces) of fluid per 24 hours. Asymptomatic, predominantly indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia occurs in roughly 14% of patients. Indinavir is metabolized by and inhibits CYP3A4, producing extensive and sometimes life-threatening drug interactions; numerous CYP3A4-dependent drugs are contraindicated. Other concerns include hepatitis, hemolytic anemia, new-onset or worsened diabetes/hyperglycemia, fat redistribution, immune reconstitution syndrome, and tubulointerstitial nephritis. Dose is reduced in mild-moderate hepatic cirrhosis.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults, in combination with other antiretroviral agents

dosage.c: Mild-to-moderate hepatic insufficiency due to cirrhosis

admin: Take 800 mg every 8 hours at evenly spaced intervals around the clock to maintain antiviral levels and prevent resistance
For best absorption take on an empty stomach with water 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal; a high-fat/high-calorie meal cuts absorption by ~77% (AUC)
Alternatively may be taken with a light, low-fat meal (e.g., dry toast with jelly and juice, or corn flakes with skim milk) or with other liquids such as skim milk, juice, coffee, or tea
Drink at least 1.5 liters (about 48 ounces) of fluids over each 24 hours to maintain hydration and reduce the risk of kidney stones
Capsules are moisture-sensitive: keep them in the original bottle with the desiccant and store at room temperature, protected from moisture
Always use as part of a combination antiretroviral regimen; never as monotherapy
moa: HIV-1 protease is an enzyme required for proteolytic cleavage of the viral Gag and Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors into the individual functional proteins of infectious HIV-1. Indinavir is a peptidomimetic inhibitor that binds the protease active site and reversibly inhibits the enzyme. This inhibition blocks cleavage of the viral polyproteins, so that the virus produces immature, structurally disorganized, non-infectious particles, interrupting the spread of infection to new cells. In vitro the 95% inhibitory concentration ranged from 25 to 100 nM, and indinavir showed synergistic antiviral activity when combined with the nucleoside analogues zidovudine and didanosine.

absolute: Clinically significant hypersensitivity to indinavir or any component
Concomitant ergot derivatives (dihydroergotamine, ergonovine, ergotamine, methylergonovine)
Concomitant lovastatin or simvastatin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors)
Concomitant sildenafil when used for pulmonary arterial hypertension (Revatio)
Concomitant oral midazolam, triazolam, or alprazolam (sedative/hypnotics)
Concomitant St. John's wort (markedly lowers indinavir and may cause resistance) - not recommended/avoid
relative: History of nephrolithiasis or conditions favoring dehydration
Hemophilia A or B (risk of increased bleeding with protease inhibitors)
Co-administration with rifampin (strongly lowers indinavir; avoid)
monitor: Hydration status and urinalysis (crystalluria, hematuria, leukocyturia)
Serum bilirubin (especially indirect) and liver enzymes (ALT/AST)
Complete blood count / hemoglobin for hemolytic anemia
Signs of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant patients; indinavir should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Because indinavir causes asymptomatic hyperbilirubinemia, it is unknown whether administration in the perinatal period would exacerbate physiologic hyperbilirubinemia in neonates, so neonatal bilirubin warrants attention. Pharmacokinetic data in pregnancy suggest substantially reduced indinavir exposure, which is a concern for maintaining viral suppression.
lact: It is not known whether indinavir is excreted in human milk. Regardless, mothers with HIV-1 infection should NOT breastfeed because of the risk of postnatal transmission of HIV-1 to an uninfected infant.
renal: The pharmacokinetics of indinavir have not been studied in patients with renal insufficiency, and less than 20% of the drug is excreted unchanged in urine. The central renal concern is nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis from drug crystallization, which has been associated with renal insufficiency or acute renal failure; maintain adequate hydration (at least 1.5 L/24 h) and interrupt or discontinue therapy if stone-related signs (flank pain, hematuria) occur. Patients with asymptomatic severe leukocyturia should be monitored for tubulointerstitial nephritis.
hepatic: Patients with mild-to-moderate hepatic insufficiency and clinical evidence of cirrhosis have decreased indinavir metabolism, with roughly 60% higher mean AUC after a single dose and half-life increased to about 2.8 hours; reduce the dose to 600 mg every 8 hours. Indinavir pharmacokinetics have not been studied in severe hepatic insufficiency. Hepatitis, including fatal hepatic failure, has been reported.

major: Contraindicated CYP3A4 substrates - alfuzosin, amiodarone, lurasidone, pimozide, cisapride, ergot derivatives, lovastatin, simvastatin, oral midazolam, triazolam, alprazolam, and sildenafil (for PAH): risk of serious/life-threatening toxicity
St. John's wort - substantially decreases indinavir concentrations and may cause loss of virologic response and resistance; avoid
Rifampin - potent CYP3A4 inducer that markedly lowers indinavir concentrations; avoid
Rifabutin - lowers indinavir and raises rifabutin; increase indinavir to 1000 mg q8h and halve rifabutin
Ketoconazole / itraconazole - raise indinavir concentrations; reduce indinavir to 600 mg q8h
Ritonavir - raises indinavir levels; combination with indinavir is associated with a higher incidence of nephrolithiasis
moderate: Efavirenz and nevirapine - decrease indinavir concentrations (CYP3A4 induction)
Delavirdine - increases indinavir concentrations; consider reducing indinavir to 600 mg q8h
Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin - increased risk of statin toxicity; use lowest necessary statin dose
Parenteral midazolam - increased midazolam levels; use only with close clinical monitoring
Sildenafil for erectile dysfunction - use reduced sildenafil dose with caution
Atazanavir - co-administration not recommended (additive indirect hyperbilirubinemia)
minor: Didanosine (buffered) - administer at least 1 hour apart from indinavir on an empty stomach to avoid pH-related malabsorption
interactions.food: A high-calorie, high-fat, high-protein meal reduces indinavir AUC by about 77% and Cmax by about 84%; take on an empty stomach with water, or with a light low-fat meal that does not appreciably affect absorption.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is described in the prescribing information.
interactions.diagnostics: Asymptomatic elevation of bilirubin (predominantly indirect/unconjugated, total bilirubin >=2.5 mg/dL) occurs in about 14% of patients; expect this when interpreting liver panels. Monitor urinalysis for crystalluria, hematuria, and leukocyturia.

serious: Acute renal insufficiency or renal failure from stones
New-onset or worsened diabetes mellitus / hyperglycemia (including diabetic ketoacidosis)
rare: Spontaneous bleeding in patients with hemophilia
emergency: Acute renal failure or obstructing stone with pyelonephritis/bacteremia
Severe reaction from contraindicated drug interaction (e.g., ergotism, cardiac arrhythmia)

monitoring: Hydration and urinalysis (crystalluria, hematuria, leukocyturia) for nephrolithiasis and tubulointerstitial nephritis
Serum bilirubin (total and indirect) and liver enzymes (ALT/AST) for hyperbilirubinemia and hepatitis
Fasting blood glucose and lipid profile
Complete blood count / hemoglobin for hemolytic anemia
HIV RNA viral load and CD4 count for antiretroviral efficacy
Signs of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome early in therapy
counsel: Take this medicine every 8 hours, around the clock, exactly as directed - missing doses can let the virus become resistant
Take it on an empty stomach with water 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating, or with a small low-fat snack; avoid heavy, fatty meals around your dose
Drink plenty of fluids - at least about 48 ounces (1.5 liters) a day - to help prevent kidney stones; tell your doctor about back or side pain or blood in your urine
This medicine can turn your bilirubin levels up and is generally not dangerous, but report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or belly pain
Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, herbal products (especially St. John's wort), and supplements - many drugs can cause dangerous interactions
Keep the capsules in their original bottle with the drying packet (desiccant) and protect them from moisture; do not breastfeed if you have HIV
pk: Rapidly absorbed in the fasted state; antiviral effect requires combination antiretroviral therapy
Plasma Tmax ~0.8 hour (about 48 minutes) in the fasted state
~1.8 hours (increases to ~2.8 hours in mild-moderate hepatic cirrhosis)
Short half-life requires strict every-8-hour dosing; ~60% plasma protein bound
Store at room temperature 15-30 C (59-86 F); protect from moisture and keep desiccant in the original bottle
pearls: Adequate hydration is essential - at least 1.5 L (~48 oz) fluid per 24 h - to prevent nephrolithiasis/crystalluria, the signature toxicity
Asymptomatic indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia occurs in ~14% of patients and is usually benign
Take on an empty stomach (or with a light low-fat meal) - a high-fat meal slashes absorption by ~77%
Potent CYP3A4 substrate AND inhibitor: many co-medications are outright contraindicated (statins, ergots, certain sedatives, cisapride, alfuzosin, amiodarone, St. John's wort)
Reduce dose to 600 mg q8h in mild-moderate cirrhosis and with ketoconazole/itraconazole; adjust both drugs with rifabutin
Watch for hyperglycemia/new diabetes, hemolytic anemia, hepatitis, and immune reconstitution syndrome
missed: If you miss a dose, skip it and take the next dose at your regular time - do not take two doses at once. Because indinavir must be taken every 8 hours, keeping the schedule is important; if you frequently miss doses, contact your provider, as inconsistent dosing can lead to drug resistance.
overdose: More than 60 reports of acute or chronic overdose (up to 23 times the recommended 2400 mg total daily dose) have occurred. The most common symptoms were renal (nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis, flank pain, hematuria) and gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). There is no specific antidote; management is symptomatic and supportive with attention to hydration and renal function. It is not known whether indinavir is removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis.
